newsitem.title: NAMIBIA: EU pledges support for southern Africa economies.
newsitem.headline: EU pledges support for southern Africa economies.

text.p: Foreign ministers from the European Union (EU) and 12 southern African countries opened on Monday a two-day conference called to forge closer political and economic cooperation.

Irish Foreign Minister and president of the EU Council of Ministers Dick Spring called for greater support for the 12-member Southern African Development Community (SADC) in its efforts for sustainable development and tranquility, saying the EU was committed to this programme.
"We pledge in every way possible to foster and enlarge these ties in the years ahead and to play our full part in supporting Africa in this time of change and transition," he said.
The EU, Spring said, had provided financial aid to the SADC region worth three billion ECU ($3.75 billion) in the last two years and was open to looking at other areas of cooperation.

Spring urged SADC states -- Angola, Botswana, Malawi, Mauritius, Mozambique, Zambia, Zimbabwe, Tanzania, Lesotho, Swaziland, Namibia and South Africa -- to continue liberalising their economies and working towards economic integration.
The region, he said, was bound to benefit from the leadership of South African President Nelson Mandela who was elected SADC chairman two months ago.

"We feel sure that the man who led his country out of apartheid and through a difficult transition to democracy will lead SADC with the same dedication, skill and honesty of purpose which have made him an inspiration to millions," Spring said of Mandela.
South Africa's government has often been accused of lack of commitment to regional programmes.
Spring said SADC should ensure peace and stability prevailed in the region, and praised the formation of an organ to supervise such a programme.

"With skill and wisdom, you have found the balance between the rights of sovereignity and the needs of regional stability and security," he said of SADC, which according to its executive secretary Kaire Mbuende, will be seeking more EU support on Angola and Burundi.

SADC is currently trying to help member state Angola end a 20-year conflict between the government and UNITA of veteran guerrilla fighter Jonas Savimbi, while Tanzania is at the forefront of efforts to end the crisis in Burundi.
Namibian Prime Minister Hage Geingob said in a keynote address SADC regarded the EU -- some of whose members were colonial powers in the region -- as historical allies.
"For us, the EU and its constituent nations have been allies in the SADC's struggle to remove social inequalities," he said.

Besides general political and economic cooperation, the EU-SADC foreign ministers' meeting is also scheduled to discuss the consolidation of democracy in southern Africa, combating drug trafficking, clearing of region's estimated 20 million land mines and promoting trade and investment.
